o: We maintain nums2 under range-add updates while answering counting queries: how many pairs (j, k) have nums1[j] + nums2[k] == tot. Since nums1 has at most 5 elements, each type-2 query reduces to at most 5 independent questions: how many current entries of nums2 equal tot - v. The difficulty is purely data-structural: range updates plus value-histogram lookups. With n, q up to 5*10^4, recomputing a histogram per query (O(n) each) gives about 2.5*10^9 operations — too slow, motivating sqrt decomposition.
k: Because len(nums1) <= 5, a type-2 query is just 5 lookups of 'how many elements of nums2 equal some target value'.
Range add + global value histogram is awkward for a BIT or segment tree, but sqrt decomposition handles it naturally: per-block frequency maps plus per-block lazy offsets.
A lookup across blocks costs O(number of blocks), and a range update touches O(sqrt n) blocks plus O(sqrt n) individual elements.

a.i: Keep nums2 as a plain array, apply each update element-by-element, and rebuild a frequency counter on every type-2 query. Simple and correct; fine for small inputs but too slow at full constraints.
s: Apply type-1 updates directly to the array.
On a type-2 query, build a Counter of nums2 and sum counts of tot - v over v in nums1.
a.t: O(q * n) overall — each query scans or rebuilds the whole array; about 2.5*10^9 operations at max constraints, so it will TLE.
a.sp: O(n) for the array plus the counter.

a.n: Approach 2: Sqrt decomposition with per-block frequency maps
a.i: Split nums2 into blocks of size about sqrt(n). Each block stores a frequency map of its (base) values plus a lazy additive offset. A range update adjusts lazily-offset full blocks in O(1) each and rewrites at most two boundary blocks element-wise. A counting query sums, over all blocks, the frequency of (target - lazy[block]) — the lazy shift means we look up the shifted key instead of touching elements.
s: Preprocess: split the array into blocks of size B = floor(sqrt(n)); each block gets a Counter of its values and lazy = 0.

Type-1 update [x, y, val]: for each partially covered block, remove the old value (base + lazy) from its Counter, add val to the base, insert the new value; for fully covered blocks just do lazy += val.
Type-2 query tot: for each v in nums1 and each block b, add Counter[b].get(tot - v - lazy[b], 0) to the answer.
Collect answers for type-2 queries in order.
a.t: O((n + q) * sqrt(n)) — each update touches O(sqrt n) blocks/elements and each query scans O(sqrt n) blocks times at most 5 values of nums1.
a.sp: O(n) for the base array plus O(n) total entries across the per-block frequency maps.

w: Lead with the observation len(nums1) <= 5 — it collapses the pair-counting question into value-frequency lookups. The naive solution is a good sanity check but TLEs; sqrt decomposition is the intended complexity class here. Pitfalls: values grow up to roughly 10^5 + 5*10^4 * 10^5, so use 64-bit integers everywhere; delete zero-count keys to keep maps small; remember lazy offsets apply to lookups, not just updates. Follow-ups: replace sqrt blocks with a segment tree of sorted multisets, or handle point assignments instead of range adds.
